identity.title: Breadboard: The Hidden Metal Paths
identity.subject_job_sentence: A breadboard joins selected holes with hidden metal clips so circuits can be built without soldering.

learning_objectives.statement: Identify a five-hole terminal-strip group and the centre trench on the breadboard.
learning_objectives.success_criterion: I can point to a five-hole group and the centre trench.

learning_objectives.statement: Predict which holes share a hidden clip before checking.
learning_objectives.success_criterion: I can explain why two holes in the same short row are joined and two across the trench are not.

learning_objectives.statement: Verify a prediction about breadboard connectivity while unpowered.
learning_objectives.success_criterion: I can trace the connectivity map and complete the evidence card.

misconceptions.misconception: Every hole on the breadboard is joined to every other hole.
misconceptions.why_it_is_common: The dense hole grid looks uniform even though only short row segments share a clip.
misconceptions.confronted_by: The connectivity map shows the five-hole group boundary and the isolating centre trench.

vocabulary.child_definition: A short row of five holes joined by one hidden metal clip.
The gap down the middle of the board that keeps its two sides separate.

child_does: Trace the five-hole group and the trench on the map.

engage.hook: A grid of identical-looking holes hides two different kinds of connection underneath.
engage.eliciting_question: Do you think every hole on the board is connected to every other hole?

predict.question: Which holes do you think share a hidden clip with this hole?
options: the four holes beside it in the same short row
every hole in the same column

observe.what_to_observe: Which holes the cutaway diagram shows sharing one hidden metal clip, and which holes it shows the centre trench keeping apart.
evidence_fields: the five holes the cutaway shows on one clip
the two holes across the trench the cutaway shows on separate clips
the rail segment, and whether the cutaway shows a break in it

steps.action: Check with the adult that the board is not connected to any power source.
Circle your prediction for which holes share a clip.
Find one five-hole terminal-strip group on the real board.
Find the centre trench and confirm no clip crosses it.
Find one power rail segment and look for a visible break.
Trace the three locations on the connectivity map with a finger.
Tick each place found and ask the adult to verify the card.

explore.expected_observation: The cutaway shows five holes in one short row on a single clip, and no clip crossing the trench.

not_yet_outcome.symptom: The child cannot tell which five holes belong to one group.
not_yet_outcome.first_check: Recount the holes in one row segment on the map, stopping at the trench or the rail.

explain.what_you_saw: In the cutaway you saw one metal clip under five holes in a short row. You saw no clip at all crossing the centre trench. You found one rail segment and checked it for a break. The board was still disconnected.
explain.why_it_happened: A standard breadboard hides short internal metal clips under each row segment; five holes in the same segment share one clip. The centre trench is built to separate the two sides so parts with legs on both sides do not get shorted. Power rails run the long way along the edges and can be physically split partway, so a rail must be checked rather than assumed continuous.
explain.self_explanation_prompt: Tell the adult why two holes on opposite sides of the trench are never joined by the same clip.

near_transfer: Trace a different five-hole group on the same board and predict its boundary before checking.
far_transfer: A muffin tin has separate cups the way a breadboard has separate terminal-strip groups.
An ice-cube tray joins water within each separate compartment the way a terminal-strip group joins only its own five holes.

success_criteria_checklist: I can point to a five-hole group and the centre trench.
I can explain why two holes in the same short row are joined and two across the trench are not.
I can trace the connectivity map and complete the evidence card.

hinge_question.question: If you plug one leg of a part into the trench itself, is it joined to anything?
hinge_question.reveals: Whether the learner understands the trench is a gap, not a connection.

evaluate.next_lab_link: L03 uses this same connectivity picture to place jumper wires and an expansion board correctly.

identification.distinguishing_features: A rectangular board of holes in short row groups either side of a centre trench, with longer rail rows along the top and bottom edges.
identification.orientation_cue: Do not assume rail continuity from colour alone; an adult verifies the map against the physical board.

parts.label: terminal strip five-hole group
parts.role: The basic joined unit a component leg connects into.

parts.label: centre trench
parts.role: The gap that keeps the board's two sides electrically separate.

parts.label: power rail segment
parts.role: A long edge row that may be split and must be verified.

troubleshooting.what_you_notice: A part seems to connect to holes you did not expect.
troubleshooting.likely_reason: The part's legs may span more than one five-hole group.
troubleshooting.safe_first_check: With the board unpowered, recount which five-hole group each leg sits in.

troubleshooting.what_you_notice: You cannot tell if the rail is continuous across the board.
troubleshooting.likely_reason: Some breadboards physically split their rails partway.
troubleshooting.safe_first_check: Look for a visible gap in the rail line and ask the adult to confirm before relying on it.

parameters.name: terminal strip group size
parameters.condition: Each row segment on a standard breadboard is joined by one internal spring clip.

parameters.name: centre trench isolation
parameters.condition: The centre trench separates the two terminal-strip halves; no clip spans it.

quantities_taught.child_facing_meaning: Holes joined by the same hidden metal clip would let electricity pass between them if a circuit were built; today nothing is powered.

behaviour.child_level: Five holes in the same short row share one hidden metal clip, but holes across the centre trench never share a clip.
behaviour.adult_level: Standard breadboard terminal strips join five holes per row segment on each side of the centre channel; power rails run the long way and may be physically split, so continuity must be verified rather than assumed from rail colour.
behaviour.simplification_check: The child account keeps the five-hole grouping and the trench break, the two facts this lab's evidence card checks, and omits manufacturing-tolerance detail that does not change either.

failure_modes.wrong_action: Assume a power rail is continuous end-to-end without checking for a rail break.
failure_modes.consequence: A part wired to the far half of a split rail would not receive the same connection as one wired to the near half.
failure_modes.prevented_by: Trace the rail on the disconnected board and mark any visible break before relying on it.

build_map.orientation: Rails run the long way along the top and bottom edges; the centre trench runs the length of the board between its two halves.
